name: rust-lld as the default linker on x86_64 Linux (Rust 1.90)
baseline: GNU ld (BFD) called through cc, the default linker for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu before Rust 1.90
verdict_reason: The Rust project measured ripgrep's debug build: 7x less link time and 40% less end-to-end time on an incremental rebuild, and 20% less on a from-scratch build. The switch shipped in Rust 1.90.0 (2025-09-18), so x86_64 Linux users already have it.
tier_reason: The rust-lang compiler performance working group measured its own toolchain change; the post quotes one project and links the full benchmark results.
claimed_speedup: ripgrep debug build: linking 7x faster and end-to-end compile time 40% lower on an incremental rebuild; 20% lower on a from-scratch debug build
workload: ripgrep 13 built in debug mode on Linux: an incremental rebuild and a from-scratch build. The post links results for the full rustc benchmark suite.
toolchain: rustc nightly and 1.90.0 beta on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu; rust-lld compared with the system linker called through cc
platforms: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu only; other Linux targets still call the system linker by default
install: Default since Rust 1.90.0 on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu; opt out with -C linker-features=-lld
one_liner: Since Rust 1.90, rustc links x86_64 Linux programs with its bundled lld instead of GNU ld, which cuts link time several-fold.
how_it_is_fast: GNU ld dates from single-core machines and does most of its work on one thread. lld does much of its work in parallel and was built for link speed; the Rust post says some of the biggest gains come from that parallelism. The gain is largest for big binaries, binaries with a lot of debug info, and incremental rebuilds, where the linker is most of the remaining work.
use_it_when: You build on x86_64 Linux with Rust 1.90 or later: it is already on and needs no configuration
Incremental debug rebuilds, where linking is a large share of the time
skip_it_when: A crate depends on GNU ld-specific behaviour; revert with -C linker-features=-lld
Resource-constrained build machines, where the linker's parallelism competes with other work
caveats: The post quotes numbers for one project (ripgrep); the rest are on a linked results page
Hardware for the ripgrep numbers is not stated
tradeoffs: lld is not bug-for-bug compatible with GNU ld

evidence.quote: Here are more details from the ripgrep example mentioned above: for an incremental rebuild, linking is reduced 7x, resulting in a 40% reduction in end-to-end compilation times. For a from-scratch debug build, it is a 20% improvement.
Some of the big gains in performance come from parallelism, which could be undesirable in resource-constrained environments, or for heavy projects that are already reaching hardware limits.
The x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu target will now use the LLD linker for linking Rust crates by default.
